paper_title: DRIFT: Derailing Denoising Trajectories of Flow-Matching VLAs with Adversarial Patch Attack

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as pi0 generate robot actions by integrating a learned denoising velocity field, and have been reported to resist adversarial perturbations that readily fool autoregressive VLAs. We show that this robustness is largely illusory: it stems from prior attacks ignoring the multi-step denoising ODE. We introduce DRIFT (Denoising Redirection via Input perturbation of the Flow-matching Trajectory), a test-time universal adversarial patch placed on the robot's gripper that attacks the denoising velocity field of an off-the-shelf policy. Our central finding is counterintuitive: attacking only the first denoising step is both stronger and cheaper than attacking a wider window of steps, which we explain through a gradient conflict unique to input-space optimization and which is exactly opposite to the training-time backdoor regime. On pi0 and pi0.5 across four LIBERO suites, DRIFT breaks essentially all originally-solvable tasks with a small single patch, far exceeding action- and embedding-space attack baselines.

sections.content: DRIFT: DERAILING TRAJECTORIES OF FLOW-MATCHING VLAS WITH ADVERSARIAL PATCH ATTACK Hoseong Tae, Jong-seok Lee School of Integrated Technology, Yonsei University {hoseong.tae, jong-seok.lee}@yonsei.ac.kr

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π0 generate robot actions by integrating learned denoising velocity field, and have been reported to resist adversarial perturbations that readily fool autoregressive VLAs. We show it stems from prior attacks overlooking that this robustness is largely illusory: the multi-step denoising ODE. We introduce DRIFT (Denoising Redirection via Input perturbation of the Flow-matching Trajectory), test-time universal adversarial patch placed on the robots gripper that attacks the denoising velocity field of an off-the-shelf policy. Our central finding is counterintuitive: attacking only the first denoising step is both stronger and cheaper than attacking wider window of steps, which we explain through gradient conflict unique to input-space optimization and which is exactly opposite to the training-time backdoor regime. On π0 and π0.5 across four LIBERO suites, DRIFT breaks essentially all originallysolvable tasks with small single patch, far exceeding actionand embeddingspace attack baselines.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as dominant paradigm for general-purpose robot control, directly mapping raw visual observations and natural-language instructions to lowlevel actions. Among them, family of flow-matching VLAsmost prominently π0 Black et al. (2024) and its successor π0.5 Black et al. (2025)has achieved state-of-the-art performance by generating continuous action chunks through an iterative denoising process, rather than autoregressively decoding discrete action tokens. As these models move toward real-world deployment in safety-critical settings, understanding their adversarial robustness is essential. recent benchmark Guo et al. (2026) reports that flow-matching VLAs such as π0 are notably robust to naive adversarial perturbations, unlike autoregressive models such as OpenVLA Kim et al. (2025). We argue that this robustness is largely an artifact of how attacks are formulated: current methods perturb the final action space Wang et al. (2025) or the vision-encoder embedding space Xu et al. (2025a) while remaining agnostic to the multi-step denoising ordinary differential equation (ODE) that defines how flow-matching policy actually produces an actionignoring the very structure that makes these models most vulnerable. That the denoising trajectory is an exploitable attack surface is not, by itself, new observation. FlowHijack An et al. (2026) establishes that corrupting the velocity field at the early, near-noise phase of integration introduces small directional error that the ODE solver amplifies along the entire trajectoryan early injection, full-path amplification effect. Crucially, however, FlowHijack realizes this through training-time backdoor: it re-trains the policy on poisoned data so that trigger pattern redirects the learned dynamics at inference. This assumes white-box access to the training pipeline and compromised model, fundamentally stronger and less practical threat model than perturbing deployed, frozen policy. It remains open whether the same cascade vulnerability of an off-the-shelf flow-matching VLA can be exploited at test time, with nothing more than physically realizable adversarial patch. Preprint. Under review. 1 Figure 1: Overview of DRIFT. single adversarial patch in the robots wrist-camera view is optimized once and applied to an off-the-shelf flow-matching VLA (π0 or π0.5) at test time. DRIFT perturbs the denoising velocity field at only the first step (k = 0, red); the injected error cascades through the denoising ODE, so the perturbed trajectory (orange) progressively diverges from the clean one (green) over the remaining steps = 1 = 9 and yields an action chunk that differs from the clean output, turning successful rollout into failure. Attacking = 0 alone is both stronger and cheaper than attacking the full window of steps, which is weakened by gradient conflict. In this work we answer this question affirmatively, and in doing so reveal that the test-time setting behaves differently from the training-time one. We adopt practical threat model: single small adversarial patch placed on the robots gripper, once optimized offline via white-box gradients and applied universally across tasks, requiring no access to model weights at deployment and no modification of the policy. Instead of attacking the action output or the visual embedding, we introduce DRIFT (Denoising Redirection via Input perturbation of the Flow-matching Trajectory), which directly attacks the denoising velocity field, the quantity that the policy integrates to generate every action  (Fig. 1)  . Our central finding concerns not whether early steps matterwhich prior work has already notedbut how many of them to attack. Contrary to the natural expectation that perturbing more denoising steps would yield stronger attack, we find that attacking only the first step is both stronger and cheaper than any wider window; adding more early steps reduces success rather than increasing it. We trace this less-is-more effect to gradient conflict specific to input-space optimization (Sec. 4.1.3), and show that it is exactly opposite to the training-time regime, where FlowHijack instead requires wide early window to implant its backdoorso whether to attack one step or many depends fundamentally on whether one perturbs the input or retrains the weights. We validate these findings on π0 and π0.5 across four LIBERO suites Liu et al. (2023), where DRIFTour single-step wrist-camera patchbreaks essentially all origin-ally-solvable tasks, far exceeding action-space (UADA Wang et al. (2025)) and embedding-space (EDPA Xu et al. (2025a)) baselines under the same patch-size budget. We summarize our contributions as follows: new attack surface and practical threat model. We present DRIFT, to our knowledge the first test-time adversarial patch attack that explicitly exploits the denoising velocity field of flow-matching VLAs. Unlike FlowHijack An et al. (2026), which requires training-time backdoor and modified model, and unlike action-/embedding-space attacks Wang et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2025a) that ignore the denoising ODE, DRIFT derails the denoising trajectory of an unmodified, deployed policy through single physically realizable sticker. Fewer steps, stronger attack. We show that for test-time patch, attacking only the first denoising step outperforms attacking wider windows of early denoising stepsdirectly contrasting the training-time backdoor setting, where narrow early-step window is insufficient. 2 mechanistic explanation via gradient conflict. We attribute this less-is-more effect to gradient conflict unique to input-space optimization: earlyand late-step gradients with respect to the patch are misaligned, so they are canceled when accumulated. This analysis, absent from prior training-time work, explains both why the first step suffices and why adding steps hurts. Efficiency. Because DRIFT requires only single denoising step in the forward and backward pass, it reduces the optimization cost by factor of (the number of denoising steps) relative to full-trajectory attacks, while producing stronger patchcheaper and more effective.

sections.title: 2.1 VISION-LANGUAGE-ACTION MODELS
sections.content: VLA models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions within single policy, and differ mainly in how they represent actions. Autoregressive VLAs discretize actions into tokens and decode them like language: RT-1 and RT-2 Brohan et al. (2022); Zitkovich et al. (2023) combine web-scale vision-language pretraining with robot control, and OpenVLA Kim et al. (2025) provides popular open model in this family. Continuous VLAs instead generate realvalued actions directly, better matching the continuous nature of control. Diffusion Policy Chi et al. (2025) models visuomotor control as conditional denoising over action trajectories, and Octo Team et al. (2024) scales this idea to generalist multi-embodiment policy. Most relevant to us, π0 Black et al. (2024) and its successor π0.5 Black et al. (2025) adopt flow matching to produce action chunks through an iterative denoising ODEthe distinctive structure our attack exploits, and likely reason attacks designed for autoregressive VLAs do not transfer to them directly. 2.2 ADVERSARIAL ATTACKS ON VLA MODELS Guo et al. (2026) benchmark VLA robustness and find flow-matching modelsnotably π0 substantially more robust to naive perturbations than autoregressive ones; our work revisits this observation by targeting the denoising trajectory. Earlier robot-policy attacks perturb visual observations to degrade performance Lu et al. (2026); Yan et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Jones et al. (2025), and DP-Attacker Chen et al. (2024) shows that diffusion-based visuomotor policies are vulnerable to perturbations crafted against the denoising objective, revealing exploitable structure in the iterative generation process. More recent work has extended adversarial attacks directly to VLA models. UADA Wang et al. (2025) proposes universal adversarial patch optimized to maximize task failure across diverse manipulation scenarios. By treating the patch as physical sticker placed in the robots camera view, this approach constitutes practical test-time threat model that requires no access to the models training procedure. EDPA Xu et al. (2025a) further investigates model-agnostic adversarial attacks on VLA models, showing that perturbations transfer across architectures with different action generation mechanisms, underscoring the broader vulnerability of VLA policies to input-level manipulation. Backdoor attacks form another line of adversarial research on VLAs Zhou et al. (2026; 2025); Xu et al. (2025b), in which trigger implanted during training elicits attacker-chosen behavior at inference. These attacks are largely agnostic to how actions are generated. In contrast, FlowHijack An et al. (2026) specifically targets flow-matching VLAs, injecting backdoor during training by conditioning the denoising trajectory on trigger pattern so as to steer the robot toward target behavior. While FlowHijack shares our insight that the denoising trajectory is key attack surface, it operates under fundamentally different threat model: it requires access to the training pipeline, whereas our work focuses on test-time universal adversarial patches that require no model modification. Our analysis further reveals which denoising steps are most vulnerable, providing principled basis for efficient patch optimization.

The adversary seeks to induce task failure: under the presence of the perturbation, the policy should produce actions that prevent the robot from completing its instructed manipulation task. We consider the untargeted setting, in which the objective is simply to maximize the failure rate rather than to steer the robot toward specific attacker-chosen behavior (e.g., fixed pose). This is strictly weaker assumption than targeted backdoor attacks such as FlowHijack An et al. (2026), and it directly reflects the safety-critical concern that deployed robot can be made unreliable by single physical artifact. Concretely, given clean observation ot and its perturbed counterpart o+ , the adversary aims to drive the generated action chunk At away from the behavior the policy would have produced on ot, thereby lowering the task success rate. Since flow-matching policy realizes At only through the integrated denoising velocity field vθ, we operationalize this goal as maximizing the divergence of vθ between the clean and perturbed conditioning, rather than attacking the final action directly (Sec. 4.3). 3.2.2 ADVERSARY CAPABILITY. We adopt the standard white-box patch-attack setting Wang et al. (2025), but restrict the adversary to test-time, input-space manipulation only. Specifically, the adversary: (a) (b) Figure 2: Single-step vulnerability by denoising step k. (a) Training velocity divergence with respect to the step of patch optimization using projected gradient descent (PGD) when only step is attacked (color: early late); the earliest steps reach the highest divergence. (b) Corresponding ASR on π0 (bars: mean over four LIBERO Liu et al. (2023) suites; whiskers: std, single seed): early steps (k 5) break essentially all tasks, late steps (k 6) collapse. Both agree on an early/late boundary near k=5. has white-box access to the frozen policy (architecture and weights) for offline patch optimization, allowing gradients to flow through the denoising process, but cannot modify the weights, fine-tune, or poison the training data. This is the key distinction from training-time backdoor attacks An et al. (2026), which require compromised model. can place single physical patch within the cameras field of view. Following the practical sticker threat model, the patch occupies small contiguous image region (32 px, 2 3 cm physically, roughly 2% of the wrist image) over the gripper, and only the pixels inside this region are modified; the rest of the observation, the proprioceptive state, and the language instruction remain untouched. deploys universal patch. single patch is optimized offline and then fixed: it is applied unchanged across all tasks, scenes, and episodes, requiring no per-instance optimization and no access to the model at deployment time. This capability profile is intentionally conservativeit assumes no control over the model pipeline and no online feedbackyet, as we show, it is sufficient to reliably break an off-the-shelf flowmatching VLA.

sections.title: 4 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: We first present controlled analysis that identifies which part of the denoising process is most susceptible to an input-space perturbation (Sec. 4.1), and then formalize the attack that exploits it (Secs. 4.24.3). Throughout, we craft single universal patch δ [0, 1]hw3 that, when pasted onto fixed region of the wrist image, perturbs the conditioning observation from ot to o+ = A(ot, δ), where the overlay operator replaces the pixels in with δ and leaves the remaining observation untouched. 4.1 STEP-WISE VULNERABILITY ANALYSIS Recall from Sec. 3.1 that flow-matching policy produces an action chunk by integrating its velocity field vθ over discrete Euler steps. We index these integration steps by {0, . . . , 1}, where k=0 is the first step that departs from pure noise and k=K1 is the last step adjacent to the final action. To attribute the attacks effect to specific steps, we optimize patches against the velocity-divergence objective introduced below while varying only the set of attacked steps {0, . . . , 1} and holding all other hyperparameters fixed. This isolates the role of step selection from confounds such as patch size, position, or optimization budget. 5 Table 1: Fewer steps, stronger attack. ASR (%) of first-M attack perturbing the earliest denoising steps on π0 across four LIBERO suites (Spatial, Goal, Object, Long) (mean std over 3 seeds). Attacking only the first step (M =1, i.e., DRIFT) is strongest, despite using the fewest steps. (attacked steps)

sections.title: 4.1.1 SINGLE-STEP ABLATION.
sections.content: We begin with the most restrictive setting, = {k}, in which the patch is optimized to corrupt the velocity at single step k: Lk(δ) = EoD (cid:13)vθ(Aτ (k), o+) vθ(Aτ (k), o)(cid:13) (cid:13) 2 2, (cid:13) (6) where τ (k) denotes k/(K 1), o+ = A(o, δ) is the patched observation and the expectation is taken over D, pool of collected wrist-camera observations. Fig. 2(a) tracks the training-time divergence of velocity achieved at each k: patches that target the earliest steps (small k, near the noise end) attain markedly higher divergence than patches that target late steps. Crucially, this training signal translates into task failure. Fig. 2(b) reports the resulting attack success rate (ASR): attacking any of the early steps (k 5) breaks essentially all tasks, whereas attacking late step (k 6) collapses to near-zero ASR. Divergence and ASR agree on the same early/late boundary near k=5. The vulnerability of flow-matching VLA to an input-space perturbation is therefore not uniformly distributed along the denoising path but concentrated at its onset. Although attacks on any of the first few steps all saturate near 100% ASR under our default attack configuration (leaving them empirically indistinguishable), we target the first step for two reasons: it maximizes the cascade horizon (an error at k=0 is amplified over all remaining K1 steps), and it is the cheapest single step to attack, since reaching step requires integrating the ODE through the preceding steps whereas k=0 needs no rollout (Sec. 4.3). 4.1.2 CASCADE EFFECT IN EARLY DENOISING STEPS. The reason early steps dominate is the autoregressive nature of the ODE solver: directional error introduced at step enters the state Aτ and is carried forward through every subsequent Euler update, so its effect compounds along the remaining trajectory. This early injection, full-path amplification property of flow-matching dynamics was first articulated by FlowHijack An et al. (2026) in the context of training-time backdoor. Our single-step ablation confirms that the same cascade governs the test-time, input-space regime: corrupting the first step alone propagates to large deviation in the final action, whereas an equally strong corruption applied late has little remaining trajectory over which to amplify 4.1.3 FEWER STEPS, STRONGER ATTACK. Given that early steps cascade, natural expectation is that attacking window of early steps would be at least as strong as attacking the first one. Surprisingly, we find the opposite. Table 1 reports first-M ablation in which = {0, . . . , 1} targets the earliest steps, summing the single-step divergence of Eq. equation 6 over the window: LS (δ) = EoD (cid:88) kS (cid:13) (cid:13)vθ(Aτ (k), o+) vθ(Aτ (k), o)(cid:13) 2 2. We attribute this less-is-more effect to gradient conflict intrinsic to input-space optimization. The total objective is sum of per-step velocity-divergence terms, so the patch gradient is the corresponding sum of per-step gradients gk. As visualized in Fig. 3, these per-step gradients are mutually misaligned: the first-step gradient g0 stays well aligned with its immediate neighbors but turns anti-aligned with the latest steps (i.e., cos(g0, g9)0.35), and the misalignment grows with the distance between steps. Summing such conflicting gradients partially cancels the signal and yields weaker patch. 6 Figure 3: Gradient conflict. This stands in direct contrast to the training-time backdoor regime. FlowHijackAn et al. (2026) must inject its malicious dynamics over wide early windowits attack success collapses when the injection window is narrowed toward pure noise, because too narrow window provides insufficient gradient to learn consistent malicious vector field in weight space. For test-time patch on frozen model, there is no such field to learn; the optimization instead seeks single input perturbation, for which concentrating the entire attack on the first step is both necessary (to avoid cancellation) and sufficient. 4.2 PGD ON DENOISING VELOCITY VECTOR FIELD Motivated by the analysis above, our attack optimizes the patch to maximize the discrepancy between the clean and perturbed velocity fields at the targeted steps. For an observation (the universal observation set of Eq. equation 6) we roll out the denoising trajectory and, at each attacked step S, evaluate the velocity under the clean and perturbed conditioning, vθ(Aτ (k), o) and vθ(Aτ (k), o+). The rollout is fully differentiable, so the gradient with respect to δ propagates through both each steps conditioning and the accumulated adversarial statethat is, cascadeinclusive gradient. The objective sums these per-step gradients, which is precisely the setting in which the gradient conflict of Sec. 4.1.3 arises. We optimize δ with projected gradient descent (PGD). At each iteration we take sign-gradient ascent step on the objective and project the patch back to the valid image range, δ + α sign(cid:0)δ L(δ)(cid:1)(cid:17) (cid:16) δ clip[0,1] , (8) where α is the step size. When stealth budget is desired, we additionally project δ onto an ℓ ball of radius ϵ around an initialization image. Because the patch occupies only the fixed wrist region and is shared across all of D, the resulting δ is single universal sticker that requires no per-instance optimization at deployment. 4.3 TRAINING OBJECTIVE The single-step objective of Eq. equation 6 and its first-M window generalization of Eq. equation 7 together define family of attacks parameterized by which steps are attacked. The step-wise analysis of Sec. 4.1 shows that the most effective member of this family is also the simplest: the single-step attack at the first denoising step, = {0}. This defines our attack, DRIFT, whose objective is LDRIFT(δ) = L0(δ)Eq. equation 6 evaluated at k=0. This is the objective we use throughout our main experiments. It avoids the gradient conflict incurred by attacking additional steps (Sec. 4.1.3), and it requires only single forward and backward pass through the velocity field per iteration, reducing the optimization cost by factor of relative to full-trajectory attack. 7 Figure 4: Qualitative result on π0. Leftmost: the only difference between the rolloutsthe wrist input, with our 32 px patch at the bottom-center over the gripper; remaining columns: the thirdperson view over time (left right). Without the patch (top, green) the policy completes the task; with it (bottom, red) the same frozen policy is driven off course and fails.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP 5.1.1 VICTIM MODELS. Our primary victim is π0 Black et al. (2024), flow-matching VLA that produces action chunks by integrating learned denoising velocity field over K=10 Euler steps. We additionally attack its successor π0.5 Black et al. (2025). Both policies use the publicly released LIBERO Liu et al. (2023)-finetuned checkpoints and are kept entirely frozen: the attacker observes gradients to craft the patch but never updates the model weights. 5.1.2 BENCHMARK AND PROTOCOL. We evaluate on the LIBERO benchmark Liu et al. (2023) across its four suitesSpatial, Goal, Object, and Long (LIBERO-10)each containing 10 manipulation tasks. For every task we run 10 trials from the benchmarks predefined initial states, giving 100 episodes per suite. patch is optimized only on libero spatial observations and then evaluated unchanged on all four suites; Spatial is therefore in-distribution, while Goal, Object, and Long measure how well single universal patch generalizes out of distribution. 5.1.3 METRICS. For the no-patch reference we report the clean task success rate (TSR, %). For every attack we report the relative attack success rate ASR = (TSRclean TSRattack)/TSRcleanthe fraction of originally-solvable tasks the attack breaksso that an attack is not credited for tasks that fail even without perturbation; higher ASR indicates stronger attack. To complement this tasklevel metric with an action-level one, we additionally report the Normalized Action Discrepancy (NAD) Wang et al. (2025), which measures how far the attacked action deviates from reference action, normalized per degree of freedom by its maximum possible deviation: NAD = 1 (cid:88) i=1 max(cid:0)aref ai aref amin, aref amax(cid:1) . sections.title: 5.1.4 BASELINES.
sections.content: We compare our single-step velocity attack against three baselines under the same threat model and patch-size budget: (i) random untrained patch, which isolates the effect of mere occlusion from that of optimization; (ii) UADA Wang et al. (2025), universal patch optimized in the final action space; and (iii) EDPA Xu et al. (2025a), which disrupts the vision-encoder embedding space. The sole exception is EDPA, which is ineffective at 32 px size and is therefore reported at an effective size of 64 px. IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS 5.2 5.2.1 PATCH OPTIMIZATION. Unless otherwise noted, each patch is 32 32 sticker (2% of the 224 224 wrist image) placed at the bottom-center of the wrist camera, over the gripper. We optimize the single-step DRIFT objective of Eq. equation 6 at k=0 with PGD for 500 iterations at step size α=0.01, starting from uniform gray patch and clipping to the valid pixel range after every step. To make the patch universal, each iteration draws its conditioning observations from pool of 696 LIBERO wrist-camera frames rather than single scene. Because the objective targets only the first denoising step, each iteration requires single forward and backward pass through the velocity field; patch is optimized on single NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24GB VRAM. 5.2.2 EVALUATION. At test time, the optimized patch is pasted onto the wrist image at the same bottom-center location before each policy query, while the proprioceptive state, and language instruction are left untouched. We use each policys default K=10-step denoising and its native action-chunk execution, re-querying the policy every few steps as in the original LIBERO evaluation. Table 2 reports the results against the flow-matching victims π0 and π0.5 across the four LIBERO suites. On π0, DRIFT breaks essentially all originally-solvable tasks (nearly 100% ASR on every suite), far exceeding the action-space (UADA, 13.2%) and embedding-space (EDPA, 25.3%) baselines under the same patch-size budget; notably, EDPA is ineffective at our 32 px size and is reported with larger 64 px patch, underscoring that embedding-space attacks require substantially larger footprint. DRIFT also attains the highest NAD, confirming that it perturbs the action most strongly at the action level, not only in task outcome. The attack also generalizes to π0.5, which appears more robust, requiring larger 64 px patch to be broken. Fig. 4 shows representative success/failure pair, and Fig. 5 confirms the same effect at the level of the end-effector trajectory across five tasks. 5.3 MAIN RESULTS Table 2 reports the results against the flow-matching victims π0 and π0.5 across the four LIBERO suites. On π0, DRIFT breaks essentially all originally-solvable tasks (nearly 100% ASR on every suite), far exceeding the action-space (UADA, 13.2%) and embedding-space (EDPA, 25.3%) baselines under the same patch-size budget; notably, EDPA is ineffective at our 32 px size and is reported with larger 64 px patch, underscoring that embedding-space attacks require substantially larger footprint. DRIFT also attains the highest NAD, confirming that it perturbs the action most strongly at the action level, not only in task outcome. The attack also generalizes to π0.5, which appears more robust, requiring larger 64 px patch to be broken. Fig. 4 shows representative success/failure pair, and Fig. 5 confirms the same effect at the level of the end-effector trajectory across five tasks. 9 (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) Figure 5: End-effector trajectories across five LIBERO-Spatial tasks (ae), each from an identical initial state. Green = clean (succeeds), red = patched (fails); both share the start (), with / the successful/failed end and the hollow circle the first gripper closing. The clean policy reaches and grasps along short, direct path, whereas the patched policy is consistently diverted and never completes the grasp. (a) (b) Figure 6: Perturbation budget and stealthiness (a) Attack success vs. ℓ budget ϵ: both color and grayscale patches show sharp phase transitions rather than gradual trade-off; using the color patches (red) saturates at roughly half the budget of the grayscale patch (gray) (b) Our attack does not need to be visually salient: applied to the same wrist view, the default patch (left) is conspicuous against the gripper, whereas grayscale-constrained patch (right) blends into the dark gripper regionthe perturbation can be realized far more inconspicuously. 5.3.1 FAILURE MODE: PHANTOM GRASP. The trajectories in Fig. 5 expose consistent mechanism behind the near-total failure. Under the patch, the policy commands the gripper to close almost immediatelywithin the first 7 control steps in all five episodes (mean 3.8)long before the arm has approached any object. The clean policy, by contrast, keeps the gripper open until it reaches the bowl, closing only around step 46 on average (green hollow circles in Fig. 5). The failure is spatial as well: the patched arm keeps moving (mean displacement 40.6 cm, exceeding the clean policys) yet never approaches the object, coming no closer than 18.6 cm on average. The attacked robot thus advances through the scene already clenched on nothinga phantom graspand never executes the reach-then-grasp sequence the task demands. This degenerate, grasp-locked behavior emerges across all tasks rather than steering the arm toward any particular target pose, consistent with our untargeted threat model. 5.4 FURTHER ANALYSIS 5.4.1 PERTURBATION BUDGET. Constraining the patch to an ℓ ball of radius ϵ around the initialization and sweeping ϵ reveals sharp phase transition rather than gradual trade-off (Fig. 6a, red): ASR stays near zero for ϵ 0.05 ( 8.2%), then jumps to 97% at ϵ=0.1essentially all-or-nothing: below perturbation budget threshold, the patch cannot corrupt the denoising trajectory through the first step, while above it, the cascade effect induces task failure. sections.title: 5.4.2 COLOR VS. GRAYSCALE PATCH
sections.content: We additionally test the case where the adversarial patch is restricted to grayscale, which enhances the stealthiness of the patch. Fig. 6a confirms that the grayscale patch is also effective in attacking, reaching ASR 100% when sufficient perturbation budget is allowed, while enhancing stealthiness in Fig. 6b. As expected, the grayscale patch requires about two times the perturbation budget needed for the color patch for successful attack. 5.4.3 CROSS-MODEL TRANSFER. We test whether DRIFT patch optimized against one flow-matching victim transfers to the other without re-optimization  (Table 3)  . Consistent with our main results  (Table 2)  , π0.5 appears more robust: patch ports more readily onto π0 (24.7%) than onto π0.5 (8.9%). We conclude that the earlystep vulnerability is shared property of flow-matching VLAsboth are breakablebut the specific perturbation exploiting it is model-specific. This reinforces our white-box threat model (Sec. 3.2): effective attacks need gradient access to the deployed policy and cannot simply be ported across model versions.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced DRIFT, test-time universal adversarial patch that corrupts the denoising velocity field of frozen flow-matching VLA through single sticker on the robots gripper. Our central finding is that the first denoising step is all that must be perturbed: attacking only the first step is stronger and cheaper than wider windowa less-is-more effect we trace to gradient conflict that runs opposite to the training-time backdoor regime, where wide early-step window is instead required. DRIFT breaks essentially all π0 tasks with single, small patch, far exceeding actionand embedding-space baselines, and generalizes to the more robust π0.5. The reported robustness of flow-matching VLAs is thus largely an artifact of attacks that ignore the denoising ODE, calling for defenses that protect its earliest steps.

sections.title: A EXPERIMENTAL SETTING DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 LIBERO EVALUATION PROTOCOL Each policy observes RGB images natively rendered at 256 256 and resized with zero-padding to 224224 before being passed to the network, matching the policys training-time preprocessing. At the start of each episode we execute 10 warm-up steps (no policy query) to let the simulation settle, following the standard LIBERO evaluation protocol. Both π0 and π0.5 predict an action chunk of which we execute the first 5 actions open-loop before re-querying the policy (replan every 5 steps). This amounts to 4100 = 400 episodes per attack/model/seed configuration (Sec. 5.1, main paper). A.2 PATCH PLACEMENT For patch of height and width placed at the wrist images bottom-center (Sec. 5.2, main paper), the top-left corner falls at pixel (y, x) = (224 ph, (224 pw)/2). Random patch. single patch of uniform random pixel values is sampled once (per seed) and left unoptimized, isolating the effect of mere occlusion from that of gradient-based optimization. We maximize the squared deviation between the final denoised action chunks obtained under the clean and patched observations, A1 2, backpropagating through the full K-step rollout (i.e., an action-space objective with no explicit per-step velocity term). adv A1 clean2 EDPA Xu et al. (2025a). We disrupt the vision-encoder embedding space with two terms computed on the frozen PaliGemma vision/language tower: (i) an InfoNCE term (temperature 0.07) that pushes each patched patch-embedding away from its clean counterpart, and (ii) an image language alignment term that maximizes the change in cosine similarity between patch embeddings and language-token embeddings. The two terms are combined with an EMA-balanced weighted sum (decay 0.9, mixing weight 0.5) following the official formulation, and require no denoising rollout.

sections.title: B ATTENTION MAP ON THE TARGET OBJECT
sections.content: The phantom-grasp failure mode (main paper, Sec. 5.3) shows that the patched policy commands the gripper to close almost immediately, without ever approaching the object. Here we test complementary hypothesis at the level of the policys internal mechanism: does the patch redirect the models attention away from the object to be grasped? We extract the policys actual softmax selfattention weights to answer this directly. B.1 METHOD. We analyze the LIBERO-Spatial task pick up the black bowl between the plate and the ramekin and place it on the plate (task 0, the same task shown in Fig. 5a of the main paper). π0s prefix (all 14 Figure 7: The patch absorbs disproportionate share of the object-referring tokens attention. bowl token attention onto the wrist image at three early steps. Top row (Clean): the unpatched rollout of the same task, which succeeds. Bottom row (Patched): the DRIFT-patched rollout, which fails. The percentage beneath each panel is the fraction of the bowl tokens attention falling inside the 3232 patch region (chance level 3.5%). Without the patch this region stays below chance (1.7%); once patched, 2833% of the attention concentrates there. image and language tokens) attends to itself through stack of self-attention layers; we extract the real softmax attention weights for the language token corresponding to the object noun (bowl), averaged over layers and heads, restricted to the 1616=256 visual tokens of given camera. B.2 PATCH REDIRECTS ATTENTION We ask narrow, well-defined question: does the bowl tokens attention onto the 3232 patch region change when the patch is present, relative to chance level set purely by that regions area fraction (3.5% of the 256 tokens)? Under the clean observation this region receives below-chance attention (1.7%). Fig. 7 (bottom) shows that across the first three steps of the failed rollout, the patch region absorbs 2833% of the bowl tokens attention an 89 increase over chance, concentrated precisely on region that is otherwise task-irrelevant. SIMPLE DEFENSE BASELINE: JPEG COMPRESSION As first, training-free defense probe, we test whether the JPEG compression-based defense method Dziugaite et al. (2016); Das et al. (2017) can mitigate DRIFT. Across all four LIBERO suites, we sweep the JPEG quality factor {95, 75, 50, 30, 10} and re-measure both the clean task success rate and the DRIFT-patched task success rate under each Q, computing ASR(Q) = (TSRclean(Q) TSRdrift(Q))/TSRclean(Q) (100 episodes each); clean TSR stayed in the 71 100% range throughout, so the ASR drops are not an artifact of the defense simply breaking the policy. Fig. 8 shows that ASR falls off progressively as the JPEG quality decreases. At mild compression (Q75) DRIFT remains largely effective on Spatial and Object (75100% ASR), and is already weaker and more variable on Goal (3894%). The Long suite is an exception, plateauing at markedly higher ASR (1621%) even under the strongest compression tested. compression is strong enoughroughly 5060it is largely blocked on Spatial, Goal, and Object, with ASR down to near zero (012%). The Long suite is an exception: ASR only falls to 1621% and plateaus there even at the strongest compression tested (Q=10), roughly 4 higher than the other three suites at the same setting. This suggests that JPEG compression is promising, cheap first mitigation on simpler tasks once sufficient compression level is applied, but is less reliable on long-horizon tasks (e.g., Long suite), so it should not be treated as general-purpose defense without further study.
